query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Shifting the powder feedstock size distribution upward—to include a higher fraction of larger particles rather than just the currently used fine distribution—will enable thicker thermal-sprayed bond coats while keeping oxidation minimal and coating integrity high. This effect is achieved through enhanced droplet melting and splat formation that improve material build-up.
generation.material_initial_state: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited using 15–45 μm gas-atomized powder that fails to achieve the required thickness, though with minimal as‐sprayed oxidation.
generation.intervention: Replace or modify the feedstock with a distribution that includes a higher fraction of larger particles compared to the current fine distribution, without changing the basic thermal-spray parameters.
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition (e.g., using an HVOF or equivalent system) under controlled oxygen levels and spray distances, with service conditions as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system exposed to high temperatures but moderate mechanical load.
generation.structural_mediator: Larger particles produce thicker, well-flattened molten droplets (splats) upon impact; their higher thermal mass reduces the relative oxidation due to a lower surface area-to-volume ratio and improves deposition efficiency and layer build-up.
generation.mechanism: By increasing the average particle size, the feedstock droplets carry more thermal energy and momentum, allowing for more substantial melting and faster build-up of material per pass without exposing an excessive surface area to oxidation; in effect, the larger droplets create thicker splats that, when consolidated, result in an overall thicker coating while preserving phase integrity and low oxidation levels.
generation.predicted_outcome: The as-sprayed coating will be thicker than that achieved with the 15–45 μm feedstock while maintaining comparable levels of oxidation and microstructural integrity.
generation.baseline: A coating produced from 15–45 μm powder feedstock that consistently results in a bond coat thickness below the specification, albeit with minimal in-flight oxidation.
generation.boundary: If the feedstock particles are too large (e.g., well beyond 60 μm), incomplete melting may occur, leading to poor adhesion or defects. Thus, the improvement is expected only within a moderate increase in the particle size range.
generation.uncertainty: While process dynamics and heat transfer principles support the benefit of larger particles for thicker deposit buildup, the exact quantitative thickness increase and its influence on the oxidation behavior may require further tuning and detailed parametric studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform thermal-spray coating trials under identical conditions with two feedstock types: (a) standard 15–45 μm powder and (b) modified powder with a significant fraction of particles in the 30–60 μm range. Analyze the coating build-up, thickness, oxide content, and microstructural quality.
measurements: Coating thickness measured by cross-sectional optical/SEM microscopy
Oxide content measured via XRD and EDS
Coating integrity assessed by interlamellar bonding and presence of defects (cracks or pores)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified (larger particle) feedstock does not yield a statistically significant increase in coating thickness while maintaining oxide levels and structural integrity at least comparable to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As reported in [,,,], HVOF as-sprayed AlTiCrFeCoNi coatings possessed a dense microstructure and a high microhardness over 750 HV with a good fracture toughness. The heat-treated NiCoFeCrSiAlTi coating exhibits a hardness even higher than 800 HV, good wear resistance, and oxidation resistance at 1100 °C, similar to that of MCrAlY coating []. The cavitation erosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi coating is about 3.5 times that of 06Cr13Ni5Mo steel in the same environment []. The high wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA at elevated temperatures is associated with oxidation behavior. The formation of a compact oxide layer on the AlCoCrFeNi and AlTiCrFeCoNi HVOF coatings accounts for enhanced wear resistance at temperatures ≥ 800 °C [] and a lowered coefficient of friction due to its function as a solid lubricant []. In [], it was found that additions of Nd and Mo to a AlCrFeCoNi base significantly reduced the wear depth at increasing temperatures due to improved oxide layer adhesion. Thus, AlCoCrFeNiMo coatings deposited using HVOF are suitable for high-temperature application. cited_evidence.text: During mechanical alloying, the flowability of the powders also changed significantly. Due to its near-equiaxed shape and appropriate particle size distribution, the powder milled for 10 h possessed a good flowability, and can be used as a feedstock to deposit a coating by APS. Meanwhile, the flowability of the powder milled for 5 h was limited by its near-flat shape. Although the powders milled for 20 and 30 h had a shape that was nearly spherical, the appearance of the fine particles can also deteriorate their flowability. Therefore, the shape and the particle size distribution of the powders can significantly affect the flowability.
